title: Tony's Pizza goes big: umbrella, bonds, surplus lines and flood
summary: Tony opens a riverside pizzeria with a bar: umbrella vs excess, specialty liability, surety bonds, Michigan surplus lines, NFIP flood and SIRs.
objectives: Tell umbrella from excess and match specialty liability coverages to claims
Name the three parties to a surety bond and the main bond types
Know Michigan's surplus lines rules and the NFIP limits, wait and deductibles
Explain how a self-insured retention differs from a deductible

scenes.title: Tony's Pizza goes big
scenes.subtitle: 4% of your exam, about 6 questions: umbrellas, specialty liability, bonds, surplus lines, flood

scenes.title: Umbrella vs excess liability
scenes.src: IRMI glossary 'umbrella liability policy', 'follow form', 'excess liability policy'; confusion pair cp_commercial-09
scenes.plain: Extra liability limits over your other policies, plus some claims they don't cover, after a self-insured retention you pay first.
scenes.example: A huge suit tops Tony's CGL limit; the umbrella pays above it. If his CGL aggregate is used up, it drops down.
scenes.exam: Pays a claim the primary policy doesn't cover? Umbrella. Only adds limits, on the underlying terms? Excess (follow form).

beats.text: First, bigger lawsuits. An umbrella adds extra liability limits over your other policies. For Tony, it sits on top of his CGL, adding limits when the underlying ones run out.
beats.say: First, bigger lawsuits. An umbrella adds extra liability limits over your other policies. For Tony, it sits on top of his C G L, adding limits when the underlying ones run out.

beats.text: Say a huge suit tops his CGL limit: the umbrella pays above it. And if a bad year uses up his CGL aggregate, the umbrella drops down in its place. It even covers some claims the CGL doesn't, after a self-insured retention Tony pays first.
beats.say: Say a huge suit tops his C G L limit: the umbrella pays above it. And if a bad year uses up his C G L aggregate, the umbrella drops down in its place. It even covers some claims the C G L doesn't, after a self-insured retention Tony pays first.

beats.text: Watch out: an excess, or follow form, policy generally follows the underlying terms. It only adds limits. So if a policy pays a claim the primary policy doesn't cover, it's an umbrella.
beats.say: Watch out: an excess, or follow form, policy generally follows the underlying terms. It only adds limits. So if a policy pays a claim the primary policy doesn't cover, it's an umbrella.

scenes.title: New business, new kinds of claims
scenes.src: IRMI glossary (E&O, D&O Sides A-C, fiduciary liability, EPLI); ISO CG 00 33 04 13; MCL 436.1803(1); hook mn_comm-25; question comm-062

spots.label: Dana: errors and omissions
spots.text: E&O covers a client's financial loss from a mistake in professional duties, generally not bodily injury or property damage.

spots.label: The board: directors and officers
spots.text: Side A pays directors and officers directly: All by themselves. Side B pays Back the Business for indemnifying them. Side C covers the Corporation itself.

spots.label: Staff 401(k): fiduciary liability
spots.text: Covers errors in running employee benefit plans under ERISA, like a trustee's imprudent investment choice for the staff 401(k).

spots.label: Fired cook: EPLI
spots.text: Employment practices liability covers employment claims like discrimination, harassment and wrongful termination.

spots.label: The bar: liquor liability
spots.text: Covers injury the insured is liable for from selling or serving alcohol. Michigan retail liquor licensees must file proof of financial responsibility of at least $50,000.

beats.text: New business, new claims. Tap each glowing spot to see which policy answers.
beats.say: New business, new claims. Tap each glowing spot to see which policy answers.

reveal.text: Professional mistakes: E&O. The board's wrongful acts as directors and officers: D&O. Benefit plan errors: fiduciary. The fired cook: EPLI. Injury from serving alcohol: liquor liability.
reveal.say: Professional mistakes: E and O. The board's wrongful acts as directors and officers: D and O. Benefit plan errors: fiduciary. The fired cook: E P L I. Injury from serving alcohol: liquor liability.

reveal.text: In Michigan, retail liquor licensees must file proof of financial responsibility of at least $50,000.
reveal.say: In Michigan, retail liquor licensees must file proof of financial responsibility of at least fifty thousand dollars.

scenes.q: Tony buys a new warehouse, but Dana forgets to add it to his property policy. Two months later it burns, and he sues her. Which coverage is designed for this claim?
scenes.why: Dana's professional mistake caused Tony a financial loss, which E&O is designed to cover. A CGL covers bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury, not this.

draw.text: You never added it to my policy!

beats.text: Two months after Tony buys a new warehouse, it burns.
beats.say: Two months after Tony buys a new warehouse, it burns.

beats.text: Dana! You never added it to my property policy!
beats.say: Dana! You never added it to my property policy!

beats.text: He sues her. Which coverage is designed for this claim?
beats.say: He sues her. Which coverage is designed for this claim?

reveal.text: Errors and omissions. Tony's financial loss came from a mistake in Dana's professional duties.
reveal.say: Errors and omissions. Tony's financial loss came from a mistake in Dana's professional duties.

scenes.title: Dana's E&O plays by different rules
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: professional liability, claims-made, defense within limits, consent to settlement; ISO CG 00 01 04 13

draw.label: Error: even before the policy began
Claim made in this policy period

draw.text: We may settle at our discretion.

beats.text: Like most professional liability, Dana's E&O is claims-made: a claim made during the policy period triggers it, even for an error before the policy began.
beats.say: Like most professional liability, Dana's E and O is claims-made: a claim made during the policy period triggers it, even for an error before the policy began.

beats.text: Like most, it lets defense costs shrink the limit, leaving less for damages: shrinking limits.
beats.say: Like most, it lets defense costs shrink the limit, leaving less for damages: shrinking limits.

beats.text: And it has a consent to settlement, or hammer, clause: the insurer must seek Dana's approval before settling.
beats.say: And it has a consent to settlement, or hammer, clause: the insurer must seek Dana's approval before settling.

beats.text: Tony's CGL pays defense on top of the limits, and the insurer may settle at its discretion.
beats.say: Tony's C G L pays defense on top of the limits, and the insurer may settle at its discretion.

scenes.title: One promise, three parties
scenes.src: FAR 48 CFR 28.001 'Bond'; surety.org; SFAA and AGC claims guide; IRMI 'surety bond'; hook mn_comm-21
scenes.plain: A three-party guarantee: the principal promises to perform, the obligee is protected, and the surety guarantees the promise.
scenes.example: Tony hires Paul to build the new place and requires a performance bond. Paul is the principal, Tony the obligee, and a surety backs Paul's promise.
scenes.exam: Unlike insurance, the surety is only secondarily liable, and the principal must reimburse it for any loss it pays.

beats.text: Now the builders. Tony hires a contractor, Paul, and requires a surety bond: one promise, three parties.
beats.say: Now the builders. Tony hires a contractor, Paul, and requires a surety bond: one promise, three parties.

beats.text: Here, it's a performance bond for building the new place. A first-letter trick: Paul, the Principal, Promises to perform. Tony, the Obligee, is Owed and protected; he required the bond. The Surety Stands behind the promise and guarantees it.
beats.say: Here, it's a performance bond for building the new place. A first-letter trick: Paul, the Principal, Promises to perform. Tony, the Obligee, is Owed and protected; he required the bond. The Surety Stands behind the promise and guarantees it.

beats.text: If the surety pays, it Sends the bill back: unlike insurance, the principal must reimburse the surety. Another difference: the surety is only secondarily liable.
beats.say: If the surety pays, it Sends the bill back: unlike insurance, the principal must reimburse the surety. Another difference: the surety is only secondarily liable.

scenes.title: Paul's call: the surety's bill
scenes.src: SFAA and AGC claims guide; surety.org; confusion pairs cp_commercial-10, -11; adapted from hook mn_comm-21

beats.text: Halfway through, Paul walks off the job. The surety pays Tony's loss, then sends Paul the bill.
beats.say: Halfway through, Paul walks off the job. The surety pays Tony's loss, then sends Paul the bill.

beats.text: A bill? For me?
beats.say: A bill? For me?
beats.speaker: Paul

options.label: Toss it. The bond was my insurance!
options.fail: The bond protected Tony, not Paul. Paul, the principal, stays primarily liable and must reimburse the surety for the loss it paid.

beats.text: Paul tosses it. But the bond protected Tony, not Paul.
beats.say: Paul tosses it. But the bond protected Tony, not Paul.

options.label: Forward it to Tony, the obligee
options.fail: The obligee is the protected party, not the one who pays. The principal, Paul, must reimburse the surety.

beats.text: Nice try, Paul. I'm the obligee. The bond protects me!
beats.say: Nice try, Paul. I'm the obligee. The bond protects me!

options.label: Pay the surety back
options.win: The surety backed Paul's promise, but Paul, the principal, stays primarily liable and repays any loss the surety pays.

beats.text: Paul pays the surety back. Next time, he finishes the job.
beats.say: Paul pays the surety back. Next time, he finishes the job.

reveal.text: Remember: the principal must reimburse the surety for any loss it pays.
reveal.say: Remember: the principal must reimburse the surety for any loss it pays.

scenes.title: Sort the bonds
scenes.src: FAR 48 CFR 28.001; IRMI glossary; FC&S 'Judicial Bonds' (2000) and 'License and Permit Bonds' (2010); hook mn_comm-21; PSI 16-81 outline

items.text: Bid bond: if Paul wins, he signs and bonds up
items.why: The bidder will sign and furnish the bonds.

items.text: A township requires it for a license
items.why: The licensee will obey the law. Township: obligee. Applicant: principal.

items.text: A court-appointed estate manager acts faithfully
items.why: Fiduciary bond: a person the court trusts with others' property acts faithfully.

items.text: Posted by a plaintiff who gets an injunction
items.why: Court bond: pays damages or costs if the bonded party's court action fails.

items.text: Payment bond: Paul's crew gets paid
items.why: Labor and material suppliers get paid.

beats.text: Your exam groups surety bonds into three families. Contract bonds back a contractor's promises; license and permit bonds, obeying the law; judicial bonds, court cases and appointments. Sort them!
beats.say: Your exam groups surety bonds into three families. Contract bonds back a contractor's promises; license and permit bonds, obeying the law; judicial bonds, court cases and appointments. Sort them!

reveal.text: Contract bonds: bid, performance and payment. On a license and permit bond, the government requiring it is the obligee, and the applicant is the principal.
reveal.say: Contract bonds: bid, performance and payment. On a license and permit bond, the government requiring it is the obligee, and the applicant is the principal.

reveal.text: Judicial bonds come in two classes. Fiduciary bonds are for people a court trusts with others' property. Court bonds, like attachment or injunction bonds, pay if the bonded party's court action fails.
reveal.say: Judicial bonds come in two classes. Fiduciary bonds are for people a court trusts with others' property. Court bonds, like attachment or injunction bonds, pay if the bonded party's court action fails.

scenes.title: When no licensed insurer says yes
scenes.plain: Insurance from an insurer not licensed in Michigan but eligible to write here, placed only by a surplus lines licensee.
scenes.example: No licensed insurer will cover the axe-throwing lane Tony is opening next door, a separate business. A surplus lines licensee can place it.
scenes.exam: Each policy: a red-ink notice in at least 10-point type. The insurer isn't licensed by Michigan; claims may not be guaranteed if it's insolvent.

beats.text: Tony is also opening an axe-throwing lane next door, as a separate business. No licensed insurer will cover it. Enter surplus lines: insurers not licensed in Michigan, but eligible to write here.
beats.say: Tony is also opening an axe-throwing lane next door, as a separate business. No licensed insurer will cover it. Enter surplus lines: insurers not licensed in Michigan, but eligible to write here.

beats.text: In Michigan, only a surplus lines licensee may place the axe lane's coverage, and only if licensed, or authorized, insurers won't write it. If 3 or more readily do, it's presumed available.
beats.say: In Michigan, only a surplus lines licensee may place the axe lane's coverage, and only if licensed, or authorized, insurers won't write it. If three or more readily do, it's presumed available.

beats.text: Each policy carries a red-ink notice, in at least 10-point type: the insurer isn't licensed by Michigan. Claims may not be guaranteed if it's insolvent.
beats.say: Each policy carries a red-ink notice, in at least ten-point type: the insurer isn't licensed by Michigan. Claims may not be guaranteed if it's insolvent.

scenes.title: Dana's call: placing Tony's coverage
scenes.src: MCL 500.1905(1), (3)(d); 500.1910(1)-(2) (federal NRRA home-state rules not reviewed); hook mn_comm-22

draw.label: Separate axe lane: no licensed insurer

draw.text: I have no surplus lines license!

beats.text: Three licensed insurers readily write the restaurant. The axe lane, a separate business? None will.
beats.say: Three licensed insurers readily write the restaurant. The axe lane, a separate business? None will.

beats.text: I have no surplus lines license. What's my move?
beats.say: I have no surplus lines license. What's my move?

options.label: Move it all to surplus lines
options.fail: In Michigan, the restaurant is its own risk that 3 or more authorized insurers readily write, so it's presumed available and stays with them.

beats.text: Nope. The restaurant's presumed available: it stays home.
beats.say: Nope. The restaurant's presumed available: it stays home.

options.label: Place the axe lane herself
options.fail: In Michigan, no one may solicit, bind or place surplus lines insurance without a surplus lines license.

beats.text: Stop! No surplus lines license, no placing it.
beats.say: Stop! No surplus lines license, no placing it.

options.label: Axe lane only: call a surplus lines licensee
options.win: In Michigan, the restaurant, readily written by 3 or more authorized insurers, stays home. The separate axe lane goes to a surplus lines licensee.

beats.text: Perfect: a licensed insurer for the restaurant, a surplus lines licensee for the axe lane.
beats.say: Perfect: a licensed insurer for the restaurant, a surplus lines licensee for the axe lane.

reveal.text: Under Michigan's statute, the surplus lines licensee pays a 2% tax plus a 0.5% regulatory fee.
reveal.say: Under Michigan's statute, the surplus lines licensee pays a two percent tax plus a zero point five percent regulatory fee.

scenes.title: Flood insurance: the NFIP numbers
scenes.src: 44 CFR 61.6; 44 CFR Pt. 61 App. A(1) III.D; FEMA brochures (07-2024; 01-2024); FEMA RR2.0 Simple Guide; amounts can change
scenes.hook: Homes: 250 and 100. Businesses: 500 and 500. Code compliance: 30 grand. The wait: 30 days, but none when you buy it as part of a loan closing.
items: Non-residential, like Tony's: $500,000 building and $500,000 contents
Increased Cost of Compliance: up to $30,000, within the building maximum
Minimum home deductibles, no pre-FIRM discount: building $1,000 ($1,250 over $100K); contents $1,000

beats.text: Next, the river. Write Your Own, or WYO, companies are private insurers that write and service National Flood Insurance Program policies in their own names.
beats.say: Next, the river. Write Your Own, or W Y O, companies are private insurers that write and service National Flood Insurance Program policies in their own names.

beats.text: The federal government pays all losses. Same coverage as FEMA's own NFIP Direct.
beats.say: The federal government pays all losses. Same coverage as FEMA's own N F I P Direct.

beats.text: The hook: homes, 250 and 100. Businesses, 500 and 500. Code compliance, 30 grand. The wait, 30 days, but none when you buy it as part of a loan closing.
beats.say: The hook: homes, two hundred fifty and one hundred. Businesses, five hundred and five hundred. Code compliance, thirty grand. The wait, thirty days, but none when you buy it as part of a loan closing.

beats.text: Homes means single-family and 2 to 4 family buildings. Increased Cost of Compliance pays up to $30,000 to elevate, demolish, relocate or floodproof. But building plus it can't exceed the building maximum.
beats.say: Homes means single-family and two to four family buildings. Increased Cost of Compliance pays up to thirty thousand dollars to elevate, demolish, relocate or floodproof. But building plus it can't exceed the building maximum.

beats.text: FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 sets minimum deductibles, which can change.
beats.say: FEMA's Risk Rating two point zero sets minimum deductibles, which can change.

beats.text: A home with no pre-FIRM discount: building $1,000, or $1,250 above $100,000 of coverage. Contents: a separate $1,000.
beats.say: A home with no pre-firm discount: building one thousand dollars, or one thousand two hundred fifty dollars above one hundred thousand dollars of coverage. Contents: a separate one thousand dollars.

beats.text: Back to the hook's limits. A home can get up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on residential contents.
beats.say: Back to the hook's limits. A home can get up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars on the building and one hundred thousand dollars on residential contents.

beats.text: A non-residential building, like Tony's, can get up to $500,000 on the building and the same on contents. All these amounts can change.
beats.say: A non-residential building, like Tony's, can get up to five hundred thousand dollars on the building and the same on contents. All these amounts can change.

scenes.title: Tony's call: when to buy flood insurance

draw.text: When do you want your flood policy?

beats.text: Tony is buying the river building with a bank loan, closing Friday.
beats.say: Tony is buying the river building with a bank loan, closing Friday.

beats.text: Tony, when do you want your flood policy?
beats.say: Tony, when do you want your flood policy?

options.label: Wait until a storm is forecast
options.fail: A new flood policy typically has a 30-day wait. Bought after the closing, on its own, it can start too late.

beats.text: Weeks after the closing, a storm is forecast, and Tony finally buys a policy. Ten days later the river floods, inside his 30-day wait.
beats.say: Weeks after the closing, a storm is forecast, and Tony finally buys a policy. Ten days later the river floods, inside his thirty-day wait.

options.label: Buy it at Friday's loan closing
options.win: Bought in connection with making a loan, flood coverage has no waiting period. It starts at the loan closing.

beats.text: Smart. Bought with the loan, it starts at closing.
beats.say: Smart. Bought with the loan, it starts at closing.

reveal.text: The loan exception covers making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan.
reveal.say: The loan exception covers making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan.

scenes.title: No wait, 1 day or 30 days?
scenes.src: 44 CFR 61.11(a)-(d); agents.floodsmart.gov 'Flood Insurance 101'; question comm-072; card 'NFIP waiting period'

cards.text: Sam and Jen increase their mortgage loan and buy flood coverage as part of it.
cards.why: Bought in connection with making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan: no waiting period.

cards.text: Grandma buys a brand-new flood policy on her own. No loan, no new flood map, no wildfire.
cards.why: No exception applies, so the usual 30-day wait.

cards.text: A new flood map takes effect, putting Rosa's house in a special flood hazard area. She buys 2 months later.
cards.why: Policy bought within 13 months after the new map takes effect: a 1-day wait.

cards.text: Flooding from burned federal land threatens a cabin. The owner buys within 60 days of the fire's containment.
cards.why: Policy bought within 60 days of the fire's containment: a 1-day wait.

beats.text: Two exceptions have just a 1-day wait. One: a building newly mapped into a special flood hazard area, with the policy bought within 13 months after the new map takes effect.
beats.say: Two exceptions have just a one-day wait. One: a building newly mapped into a special flood hazard area, with the policy bought within thirteen months after the new map takes effect.

beats.text: Two: flooding from burned federal land, with the policy bought within 60 days of the fire's containment.
beats.say: Two: flooding from burned federal land, with the policy bought within sixty days of the fire's containment.

beats.text: Your turn: how long does each policy wait?
beats.say: Your turn: how long does each policy wait?

reveal.text: Added coverage on a renewal bill is an exception too.
reveal.say: Added coverage on a renewal bill is an exception too.

draw.text: on a $100,000 claim: defense and damages
on a $100,000 claim: defense and damages

beats.text: Last, self-insurance: a formal decision to keep a risk and pay losses from a set-aside fund.
beats.say: Last, self-insurance: a formal decision to keep a risk and pay losses from a set-aside fund.

beats.text: Say a covered liability claim costs $100,000 in defense and damages. With a self-insured retention of $25,000, Tony pays the first $25,000 himself, and the insurer the other $75,000.
beats.say: Say a covered liability claim costs one hundred thousand dollars in defense and damages. With a self-insured retention of twenty-five thousand dollars, Tony pays the first twenty-five thousand dollars himself, and the insurer the other seventy-five thousand dollars.

beats.text: With a deductible of $25,000, the insurer pays all $100,000 first, then bills Tony $25,000.
beats.say: With a deductible of twenty-five thousand dollars, the insurer pays all one hundred thousand dollars first, then bills Tony twenty-five thousand dollars.

items: Umbrella: more limits, drop-down, fills some gaps; excess: limits only
E&O: clients' financial loss from mistakes; most PL is claims-made
Bonds: principal promises, obligee protected, surety guarantees
Michigan surplus lines: red-ink notice; 2% tax plus 0.5% fee
NFIP homes: $250K and $100K; usual 30-day wait, none at loan closing

beats.text: What a launch! Tony is ready.
beats.say: What a launch! Tony is ready.

beats.say: Now, who wants a slice?

beats.text: Before you grab one, a quick recap. An umbrella adds more limits, drops down, and fills some gaps; excess adds limits only. E&O covers clients' financial loss from mistakes, and most professional liability is claims-made.
beats.say: Before you grab one, a quick recap. An umbrella adds more limits, drops down, and fills some gaps; excess adds limits only. E and O covers clients' financial loss from mistakes, and most professional liability is claims-made.

beats.text: In a bond, the principal promises, the obligee is protected, and the surety guarantees. In Michigan, surplus lines policies carry a red-ink notice, and the surplus lines tax is 2%, plus a 0.5% fee.
beats.say: In a bond, the principal promises, the obligee is protected, and the surety guarantees. In Michigan, surplus lines policies carry a red-ink notice, and the surplus lines tax is two percent, plus a zero point five percent fee.

beats.text: And NFIP homes: up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents. The usual wait is 30 days, but none when it's bought as part of a loan closing.
beats.say: And N F I P homes: up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars on the building and one hundred thousand dollars on contents. The usual wait is thirty days, but none when it's bought as part of a loan closing.
